# An RSE learning environment
:::

::: {.hero-body}
The flagship challenge of the hackathon is an open, discipline-overarching environment in which people
_learn research software engineering by doing it_ — with accounts, teams, submitted artefacts, feedback
and peer review around the material, not just the material itself.

Parts of this exist. Oxford RSE's [Gutenberg](https://www.rse.ox.ac.uk/gutenberg) is an open-source
platform with accounts, courses and progress tracking, and it is the natural starting point rather than
a competitor. What no platform yet does is close the loop between learners — group work, artefact
submission, peer assessment — or run the exercise on the hardware RSE actually targets.

This page sets out what already exists, why general-purpose learning technology does not fit RSE, and
the design questions we want to attack in Glasgow. None of them is settled — that is the point of the
two days.

## Why not just use a normal learning platform?

Learning technology has thirty years of standards and platforms behind it, and RSE should reuse every
bit of it that fits. Three things do not fit.

::: {.why-grid}

::: {.why-card}
### Notebooks are not documents
The dominant RSE teaching format is the executable notebook — Jupyter, R Markdown, Quarto. Learning
management systems assume a self-contained, assessable object: a page, a video, a quiz. A notebook is
none of these; it is code that must _run_ against a real environment before it means anything.
:::

::: {.why-card}
### Compute is part of the exercise
An RSE assignment is frequently about the machine: a [GPU]{.highlight} kernel, an [MPI]{.highlight}
job, a [SLURM]{.highlight} batch script, a container that has to build. You cannot embed "submit this
to the cluster and account for your allocation" in a quiz engine.
:::

::: {.why-card}
### Results must leave again
What a course produces — lessons, worked solutions, learner artefacts — should be publishable as open
educational resources and as reusable notebooks. Today it is either locked inside a course shell or
published as a static site with no environment around it.
:::

:::

## What already exists — and what it does not cover

The offerings closest to what we propose, with their public sources, and the gap each one leaves.

::: {.landscape}

| Environment | What it offers | What it does not cover |
|---|---|---|
| **[Gutenberg](https://www.rse.ox.ac.uk/gutenberg)** · Oxford RSE, for [UNIVERSE-HPC](http://www.universe-hpc.ac.uk/) — [GitHub](https://github.com/OxfordRSE/gutenberg), running at [train.rse.ox.ac.uk](https://train.rse.ox.ac.uk/)<br>_RSE and HPC training, undergraduate through to CPD_ | The closest thing that exists: an open-source (BSD-3) Next.js/PostgreSQL platform with user accounts, course enrolment, pathway-based syllabi, and module completion plus exercise results reported back to course leaders. Material stays as Markdown in separate CC-licensed repositories, so content and engine are decoupled and any institution can self-host | Closes the instructor-facing half of the loop only: no group formation, no submission of a learner-built artefact, no peer assessment. Exercises are Markdown callouts and no execution back-end is part of the platform — so even in an HPC curriculum, learners run the code somewhere else. No learning-object metadata |
| **[The Carpentries](https://carpentries.org/)** · Software, Data & Library Carpentry — [GitHub](https://github.com/carpentries)<br>_Cross-disciplinary foundational computing skills_ | Community-maintained open lessons, instructor training, and a global workshop network | Lesson websites plus instructor-led workshops, not a running environment: no accounts, no teams, no artefact submission, no peer assessment |
| **[RSE-Mentopolis](https://learntech.rwth-aachen.de/go/id/bmahlp/)** · RWTH Aachen / Klaus Tschira Foundation<br>_Sustainable research software: lifecycle models and educational modules_ | The closest in ambition — stakeholder and lifecycle models plus teaching modules for researchers who develop software | A research project anchored in one institution, producing models and modules rather than an environment other universities can deploy and run |
| **[KODAQS Toolbox](https://kodaqs-toolbox.gesis.org/)** · GESIS / Mannheim / LMU — built on [andrew](https://github.com/GESIS-Methods-Hub/andrew)<br>_Social sciences: data quality across survey, digital behavioural and linked data_ | Curated tutorials with hands-on coding examples in an open-source aggregation hub, alongside the blended KODAQS Academy programme | Single discipline and single topic; teaches data-analysis practice rather than software engineering. The hub aggregates content; it does not host group work |
| **[iBOTS / iBehave](https://learn.ibots-bonn.de/docs/)** · University of Bonn — [GitHub](https://github.com/ibehave-ibots)<br>_Neuroscience_ | Open, self-paced course tracks from Python and NumPy through to Git and DataLad, delivered as a static site with Jupyter notebooks | Single discipline, and static by construction: no user management, no group formation, no feedback loop, no assessment of what learners produce |

:::

_Landscape as surveyed for the CHARTED dRTP proposal; all links checked 3 August 2026._

Three gaps follow, and they are exactly what the hackathon attacks:

1. _Coverage is siloed._ Where teaching is hands-on, it is usually tied to one discipline's research process or to one technology stack. Gutenberg is the instructive exception: it is discipline-neutral precisely because the content lives in separate repositories and only the engine is shared.
2. _The loop is only half closed._ Gutenberg gets furthest — accounts, enrolment, completion and exercise results — but stops at what the instructor sees. None of these offerings covers group formation → artefact submission → structured feedback → peer assessment, so learners still never review each other's code.
3. _AI-generated code is unaddressed._ No existing environment lets a team record which parts of generated code a human actually inspected.

We build **on** this rather than duplicating it. Carpentries lessons and the KODAQS and iBOTS course
structures are directly reusable inside such an environment — and Gutenberg is a serious candidate for
the base itself: BSD-licensed, self-hostable, already carrying the accounts and course model, and
missing exactly the pieces the hackathon sets out to prototype. "Extend Gutenberg" is a legitimate
outcome of the two days, and arguably the cheapest route to a working thin slice.

## The link to learning technology: standards

Underneath the gaps sits a question that predates this proposal and comes out of the RSE curriculum
discussion: **where should RSE learning material be stored, and in which format?** The material we
surveyed lives as executable notebooks and R Markdown rendered into static sites, or as plain Markdown
in Git repositories — the *andrew* aggregator behind the KODAQS Toolbox executes Jupyter and R Markdown
inside containers, the iBOTS platform is a static site with notebooks, Gutenberg pulls CC-licensed
Markdown from separate repositories — while the learning-object metadata standards from learning
technology are absent throughout. Not one of these platforms describes its material with LOM, SCORM or
anything equivalent; discovery and reuse across institutions happen by reading READMEs.

::: {.why-grid}

::: {.why-card}
### IEEE LOM
Learning Object Metadata describes a resource so it can be found and reused across repositories. It is
the natural candidate for an RSE OER index — but its educational vocabulary (interactivity type,
typical learning time, semantic density) was written for documents, not for a code repository plus an
environment specification.
:::

::: {.why-card}
### SCORM / xAPI
Packaging and run-time tracking for self-contained courseware. SCORM assumes the object runs in the
browser inside the LMS; an RSE exercise runs in a container, or on a cluster. [xAPI]{.highlight} is the
more promising half: it can record statements about activity that happens *outside* the platform.
:::

::: {.why-card}
### H5P
Rich interactive content types, open source and widely integrated into LMSs. Excellent for the
conceptual layer of an RSE lesson; it has no notion of executing learner-supplied code against a real
toolchain. Where is the boundary between an H5P element and a notebook cell?
:::

:::

The open question for the hackathon is therefore not which standard to adopt but whether any of them
is *applicable* to RSE content at all, given that they assume self-contained, assessable objects rather
than code that must run against a real environment — and, if the answer is "partly", which profile or
extension covers the rest.

## The link to RSE requirements: real infrastructure

The other half of the problem is the one learning technology never had to solve. Gutenberg makes the
point sharply: it was built for [UNIVERSE-HPC]{.highlight}, a curriculum explicitly about research
software engineering *for high-performance computing*, by the RSE groups at Oxford, Southampton,
Imperial and Edinburgh together with EPCC and the Software Sustainability Institute — and it still
delivers material *about* HPC rather than running *on* it. The compute stays the learner's problem.
That is not an oversight in Gutenberg; it is the hard part everyone has deferred.

An RSE learning environment sits on top of research computing infrastructure, which means:

- **Compute back-ends.** Where do examples with [GPU]{.highlight} requirements run? Notebook services
  such as JupyterHub or BinderHub cover the small cases; teaching CUDA kernels or MPI means a real
  allocation on an [HPC]{.highlight} system, reached through a batch scheduler (SLURM) or a gateway
  such as Open OnDemand.
- **Identity and access.** University HPC access runs on federated identity and project allocations.
  An environment that hands out accounts has to reconcile that with how clusters actually admit users.
- **Environments as artefacts.** Containers, lockfiles and module systems are not deployment details
  here; reproducing the environment *is* part of the learning objective and part of what gets assessed.
- **Languages.** [Python and R]{.highlight} at minimum, as in *andrew* — but RSE teaching also needs
  compiled languages: [C++]{.highlight}, Fortran, Julia, and the build systems around them.
- **Cost and fair use.** Peer assessment means many people running each other's code. Quotas,
  scheduling and cost control are design constraints from day one, not afterthoughts.

## Open design questions for the two days

1. **Metadata standards.** Is any learning-object metastandard (IEEE LOM, SCORM/xAPI, H5P) applicable to RSE content? What would an RSE application profile have to add?
2. **Architecture.** Federated, so institutions keep and describe their own material — or component-based, with one platform and pluggable parts? Gutenberg has already picked an answer worth arguing with: shared engine, content in separate repositories.
3. **Runnable examples.** Which languages must be supported, and in book-style or notebook-style form?
4. **Compute.** Where do GPU and HPC examples run, and who pays for them?
5. **Integration.** How does such an environment sit alongside the learning management systems universities already run — and alongside the GitLab/GitHub instances where the code already lives?
6. **Build on, or build new?** Several groups have built their own platform — Gutenberg above all, and it is open source and self-hostable. What are their perks, can they be integrated rather than replaced, and is forking Gutenberg the fastest way to a working thin slice?
7. **AI-generated code.** How do you represent, store and assess "this block was generated, and a human inspected it"?

The [modules page](modules.html) breaks these down into pieces small enough to build in two days, and
says what we think the two days can realistically produce.

## Bring an answer — or a better question

If you have built one of these, surveyed one of these, or have strong opinions about any of the seven,
come and say so on day 1.

<button id="theme-toggle" class="theme-toggle" aria-label="Toggle light and dark mode">● Dark mode</button>
<script>
(function () {
  var root = document.documentElement;
  var btn = document.getElementById('theme-toggle');
  var stored = localStorage.getItem('theme-v2');
  function setDark() {
    root.setAttribute('data-theme', 'dark');
    btn.textContent = '☀ Light mode';
  }
  function setLight() {
    root.removeAttribute('data-theme');
    btn.textContent = '● Dark mode';
  }
  if (stored === 'dark') setDark();
  btn.addEventListener('click', function () {
    var isDark = root.getAttribute('data-theme') === 'dark';
    if (isDark) {
      setLight();
      localStorage.setItem('theme-v2', 'light');
    } else {
      setDark();
      localStorage.setItem('theme-v2', 'dark');
    }
  });
})();
</script>
